questions.q: If an implication statement is represented as $P \implies Q$, which of the following represents the contrapositive of this statement?
questions.explain: The contrapositive of an implication $P \implies Q$ is formed by negating both terms and reversing their direction. It is written as $\neg Q \implies \neg P$. A conditional statement and its contrapositive are logically equivalent.

questions.q: Given the premise 'If John studies hard, he will pass the exam,' and the fact 'John did not pass the exam,' what is the valid conclusion derived using logic?
questions.explain: This follows the rule of inference known as Modus Tollens. If $P \implies Q$ is true, and $Q$ is false ($\neg Q$), then $P$ must also be false ($\neg P$). Thus, concluding 'John did not study hard' is logically valid.

questions.q: According to the rules of truth tables, the logical conjunction statement $P \land Q$ (P AND Q) is true if and only if:
options: Both P and Q are true.
At least one of P or Q is true.
Both P and Q are false.
P is true and Q is false.
questions.explain: In boolean logic, an AND operator (conjunction) strictly requires every component to evaluate to true for the entire compound statement to evaluate to true.
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: What is the correct logical negation of the universal statement: 'All mathematicians are intelligent'?
options: Some intelligent people are not mathematicians.
questions.explain: The statement represents a universal affirmative ($\forall x, M(x) \implies I(x)$). Its exact logical negation is an existential negative statement ($\exists x, M(x) \land \neg I(x)$), which translates back to natural language as 'Some mathematicians are not intelligent' (or 'At least one mathematician is not intelligent').

questions.q: Given the premises: 'If it is raining, then the ground is wet' and the truth statement 'It is raining,' deducing the conclusion 'The ground is wet' demonstrates which rule of inference?
questions.explain: The structure 'If $P \implies Q$, and $P$ is true, therefore $Q$ is true' is the definition of Modus Ponens, also called affirming the antecedent.
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: Which logical operator symbol is standardly used to represent the biconditional statement 'If and only if'?
questions.explain: The symbol $\leftrightarrow$ signifies a two-way (bi-directional) logical relationship, meaning 'if and only if' (often abbreviated as 'iff').
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: Consider the implication: 'If a shape is a square, then it is a rectangle.' What is the converse of this statement?
options: If a shape is not a square, then it is not a rectangle.
If a shape is not a rectangle, then it is not a square.
If a shape is a rectangle, then it is a square.
A shape is a square if and only if it is a rectangle.
questions.explain: The converse of an implication $P \implies Q$ is generated by reversing the direction of the implication to $Q \implies P$. Therefore, 'If square, then rectangle' becomes 'If a shape is a rectangle, then it is a square.' Note that the converse is not necessarily factually true.

questions.q: In mathematical logic, what term defines a compound statement that always resolves to false, regardless of the individual truth values of its simple components?
questions.explain: A contradiction (also called an absurdity or a fallacy) is a statement that is unconditionally false under all possible assignments of truth values (e.g., $P \land \neg P$).
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic
questions.subject: Further Mathematics (Elective Mathematics)

questions.q: In a logical truth table, the conditional statement $P \implies Q$ is False ONLY under which of the following conditions?
options: P is True and Q is False
P is False and Q is True
P is False and Q is False
P is True and Q is True
questions.explain: A conditional statement (implication) is considered broken or 'False' only if the premise $P$ is fulfilled (True) but the conclusion $Q$ fails to happen (False). In all other cases, it evaluates to True by default.

questions.q: If a conditional statement is given as 'If $P$, then $Q$', how is its inverse constructed?
questions.explain: The inverse of an implication $P \implies Q$ is formed by keeping the order the same but negating both terms, which mathematically reads as $\neg P \implies \neg Q$ ('If not P, then not Q').
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: Which of the following propositions is logically equivalent to the implication $P \implies Q$?
questions.explain: Material implication rule states that $P \implies Q$ means 'either P is false, or Q is true'. Thus, it translates to the disjunction $\neg P \lor Q$. Evaluating truth tables for both expressions will yield identical truth values for all conditions.
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: Which logical symbol is strictly used to represent the word 'OR' (disjunction)?
questions.explain: The 'V-like' symbol $\lor$ stands for the logical OR operator (disjunction). By contrast, $\land$ is AND, $\neg$ is NOT, and $\iff$ is if and only if.
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: The statement $\neg Q \implies \neg P$ represents which relationship to the original proposition $P \implies Q$?
questions.explain: The contrapositive reverses the direction and negates both statements. So, $P \implies Q$ becomes $\neg Q \implies \neg P$. A statement is always logically equivalent to its contrapositive.
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: Which of the following compound propositions represents a tautology?
questions.explain: A tautology is a statement that is unconditionally true. By the Law of Excluded Middle, a proposition must be either true or false. Thus, 'P OR not P' ($P \lor \neg P$) covers all possibilities and is always true.
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: Consider the argument: 'If it snows, the flight will be canceled. The flight is not canceled.' What is the valid conclusion based on the rule of Modus Tollens?
questions.explain: Modus Tollens dictates that from premises $S \implies C$ and $\neg C$, we can validly conclude $\neg S$. Therefore, since the flight was not canceled, it must be logically true that it did not snow.
questions.exam: WASSCE Further Maths: Core Algebra and Logic

questions.q: Evaluate the truth value of the complex proposition $P \implies (P \lor Q)$ given that $P$ is True and $Q$ is False.
questions.explain: If P is True, the disjunction $(P \lor Q)$ evaluates to True (True OR False is True). Therefore, the implication $P \implies (P \lor Q)$ becomes True $\implies$ True, which evaluates to True.
